video_goal: Demonstrate the process of creating a natural dye from red cabbage to color white Easter eggs a vibrant blue.
required_subjects_and_props: Red cabbage, chef's knife, cutting board, stainless steel pot, water pitcher, stove, metal strainer, glass bowl, white vinegar, tablespoon, white hard-boiled eggs, slotted spoon, wire cooling rack, paper towels

outline_steps.visual_action: Hands place a vibrant head of red cabbage onto a wooden cutting board and slice it directly in half with a chef's knife.
Hands rapidly chop the red cabbage halves into smaller, jagged 1-inch pieces.
Hands scoop up the chopped red cabbage pieces and drop them into an empty stainless steel pot.
Clear water is poured from a glass pitcher into the pot, rising until it completely submerges the chopped red cabbage.
The pot sits on a lit stove burner; the water vigorously bubbles and visibly darkens into a deep purple color.
A metal strainer is held over a large glass bowl, and the contents of the pot are poured through it, catching the pale, boiled cabbage leaves while the dark purple liquid fills the bowl.
A tablespoon of clear white vinegar is poured into the steaming dark purple liquid in the glass bowl, and a metal spoon stirs the mixture in a circular motion.
Fingers place a plain white, hard-boiled egg onto the center of a metal slotted spoon.
The slotted spoon slowly lowers the white egg completely beneath the surface of the dark purple cabbage dye.
Hands gently drop three more white eggs into the bowl, where they settle at the bottom of the opaque purple liquid.
The surface of the purple liquid becomes completely still, and shadows shift rapidly across the bowl to visually indicate the passage of several hours.
The slotted spoon dips into the bowl and lifts an egg out of the liquid; the egg shell is now a vibrant, pastel blue color.
The spoon tilts, gently rolling the wet blue egg onto a wire cooling rack lined with white paper towels.
The camera slowly pans across a finished row of four dry, naturally dyed Easter eggs, highlighting their speckled blue and teal surfaces.
